“神智慧和知识的丰富，祂的判断何其深奥，祂的道路何其难测！谁知道主的心？谁曾作过他的谋士？谁先给过他，使他后来偿还？因为万有本于他，倚靠他，归于他。愿荣耀归给他，直到永永远远。阿们。”（罗马书 11:33–36）。

使徒保罗写下何等热烈而富有表现力的惊叹！当我们再次观察一首新赞美诗及其作者时，愿我们保持警醒的心和敞开的心灵，以看见神在其中的作为。

马修·布里奇斯（Matthew Bridges）于1800年7月14日出生在英格兰埃塞克斯郡的马尔登。1825年他开始发表诗作，并持续创作，直到出版了两本小型 hymns 集——《心灵的赞美诗》（Hymns of the Heart，1848）和《耶稣的受难》（The Passion of Jesus，1852）。在此，我将通过简要叙述这位诗歌作者的教会生活历史来继续故事。

我们在本文研究的这位诗歌作者曾是英格兰圣公会的一员。大约在19世纪中叶，他对所处的教会团体感到不满，跟随约翰·亨利·纽曼（John Henry Newman）领导的所谓牛津运动。根据圣诗学者阿尔伯特·贝利（Albert Bailey）的说法，该运动的核心在于“主张他们的圣公会直接承袭自原初使徒教会”。为了追求这一点，运动的追随者研究教会的古代历史、教义，尤其是礼拜形式。在此过程中，他们发现了基督教会最早几个世纪留下的丰富希腊文和拉丁文圣歌传统。

与今日我们悲哀地看到基督教会中存在许多派别类似，19世纪中叶的情况亦如此。牛津运动在某种程度上似乎是在旧与新做法之间的竞争。就我们今天故事中的人物而言，他似乎认为在保持母会旧有传统上有一条更为稳定的前路，但他同时似乎对我们的主与救主耶稣基督怀有真实而活泼的信心。此处我要插一句：我信他在良心向神的光照下做出决定，尽管我们今天从再洗礼派（Anabaptist）的观点来审视，会质疑他这样做的理由。

我们在此继续他的故事。马修·布里奇斯改宗罗马天主教，并且渴望分享新教会丰富的颂歌传统，开始创作原创赞美诗。布里奇斯的诗篇以灵性和真切的力量为标志。他的一首我们喜爱并常唱的诗是“Rise, Glorious Conqueror”。毫无疑问，他最著名的赞美诗是《以众冕冠冕祂》（Crown Him with Many Crowns）。该诗最早见于他的著作《耶稣的受难》，最初题为“The Song of the Seraphs”。

这首诗的背景颇为有趣，包括为何会有12节诗歌的来由。可以理解的是，如今只唱其中的一部分节数。节选哪些段落取决于不同的赞美诗集。

马修·布里奇斯最初于1851年撰写此歌。他写了六节，全部基于启示录 19:12：“……约有许多冠冕戴在他头上。”布里奇斯的版本流传到1870年代，这时一位虔诚的圣公会牧师戈弗雷·斯林（Godfrey Thring）出现了。戈弗雷担心这首流行的赞美诗使天主教神学的内容被新教会众所歌唱。他的担忧可能集中在布里奇斯原来第二节，那里提到了蒙福的圣母玛利亚。基于此，斯林于1874年在他的《赞美诗与圣歌词》（Hymns and Sacred Lyrics）中为这首诗写了六节新诗句并发表。

这12节诗在历年被混合搭配使用。有趣的是，如今大多数赞美诗集常见的六节中，有三节出自布里奇斯，另外三节出自斯林。该诗在《教会的赞美诗》（Hymns of the Church）一书中的发布，完全省略了布里奇斯原来的第二节，并采用了布里奇斯原作的第1、3、4节与第5、第6节的部分段落。我们在下文的节选中已标出该书所唱的诗节。同时下文也收录了斯林的六段对句。

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Bridges

以众冕冠冕祂，宝座上的羔羊；
听！天上的赞歌如何淹没了其他一切的乐声；
醒来吧，我的灵，歌颂那为你而死的祂，
向祂欢呼，作你无比的王，直到永永远远。

冠祂为童贞女之子！道成肉身的神诞生——
那臂膀赢得的绯红战利品如今装点祂的额冠！
如同那玫瑰之果，乃是玫瑰的茎：
这根永远流出怜悯的根──伯利恒的婴孩！

冠祂为和平之主！祂掌权以节杖施治，
从极到极，诸战争止息，沉浸于祈祷与赞美：
祂的国度永无穷尽，围绕祂被刺的脚下，
天堂的美丽花朵散发出永远芬芳的香气。

冠祂为慈爱之主！看祂的手和祂的肋——
富足的伤痕，至高地显于荣耀之上：
没有天使在穹苍中能尽览那景象，
却俯首观看，那般明亮的奥秘令其心炽燃！

冠祂为岁月之主！时间的元首——
创造滚动诸天的造物主，何其难以言表的崇高！
镶嵌在光海之中，永恒的波涛，
反映祂的宝座──无限者！祂活着──爱着──并拯救。

冠祂为诸天之主！与父同为一体而为人所知，
又因那三一宝座所赐的圣灵而得蒙福！
众人齐声欢呼！救赎主，万福！因祢为我而死；
祢的颂赞永不衰败，直到永远无尽！

Crown Him with Many Crowns

—Thring

以金冕冠祂，万邦大与小齐来，
冠祂吧，你们古时殉道的圣徒，曾为众被宰的羔羊；
那为他们曾被宰的羔羊，如今为那献上赞美之人——
成为冠冕之宝石，环绕祂圣洁的额头。

冠祂为神之子，在诸世界未曾起首之前，
你们这些踏过祂足迹之地的人，冠祂为人的儿子；
祂曾经历每一重使人心折的悲伤，
并将其承担为己，使众人在祂里得安息。

冠祂为光之主，祂在黑暗的世上，
身披无限荣耀的袍，展开祂烈焰的旗帜。
并高高举起，天上——地上——地下，
显示战胜撒但、罪与死的胜利之记号。

冠祂为生命之主，祂已战胜坟墓，
在为拯救祂所来之人的争战中复活得胜；
我们今歌颂祂的荣耀，祂曾死而复升，升入高处。
祂为赐永生而死，因而使死亡本身也得以灭亡。

冠祂为万主之主，祂统辖万有，
曾在地上为被赎罪人被杀的道成之言；
现今祂住在光明之境，众圣与天使同唱，
日夜在祂面前歌颂他们的神、救赎主、君王。

冠祂为诸天之主，居于上界的宝座上；
冠祂为君王，赐予祂那奇妙的名号——爱；
以众冕冠祂，当诸宝座在祂前倾倒。
你们列王也以众冕冠祂，因为祂为万王之王。

马修·布里奇斯晚年居住在加拿大魁北克省，之后返回英格兰，并于1894年10月6日辞世，享年94岁。尽管我们找不到他生平的诸多细节，但他留给我们的确是一首至为伟大的赞美诗。

这首歌长久不衰的重要原因之一在于与之配合的曲调。该副歌由乔治·乔布·埃尔维爵士（Sir George Job Elvey）在1868年为此歌特别作曲，命名为 Diademata。希腊语 diademata 一词意为“王冠”——对这激昂旋律而言，是个贴切的名称。圣诗学者 J. R. Watson 也有同感，他观察道：“Diademata为这首歌词提供了宏伟的配器，进行曲般欢欣，而从不变得机械或刺耳。”

愿我们的会众继续实践共同且全心的歌唱，在圣徒的聚会中以声音向主献上赞美！以众冕冠冕我们主耶稣基督，因为他配得！

资料来源：A Treasury of Hymn Stories, hymnary.org, umc-discipleship.org, FBC

January 21, 1525, was the 500th anniversary of Anabaptism. Five hundred years ago, a monumental event in the history of the Christian church occurred. A small group of radical Christians quietly gathered in the home of Felix Mantz in Zürich, Switzerland. The state church government of Zürich had ordered parents to have their infants baptized or face being banished from their homes. Gathering together for Scripture studies and prayer meetings was outlawed, too. Yet, on this momentous winter evening, Feliz Mantz, Conrad Grebel, George Blaurock, and a few others took their obedience one step further. After praying and committing to serve God faithfully, George Blaurock asked Conrad Grebel to baptize him in true Christian faith, which Conrad did. The others also requested baptism, and George, in turn, also baptized them. And thus, Anabaptism, as we know it, was born.

Though these three men played a key part in Anabaptist history, the Reformation did not begin with them. The real catalyst for flaming the fires of revival was kindled 88 years earlier. In 1436, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg invented a moveable type printing press. This dramatically improved printing, and books could be printed in greater quantities. Instead of a few books only in the hands of the wealthy, the common person could now afford to buy books. The first books to be printed on the Gutenberg press were Bibles. When common folks began to buy and read Bibles, they began to realize that the darkness of religious oppression was keeping them from understanding the true light of God’s Word. And thus, the Reformation was born.

Fast forward 588 years. The printed paper still inspires men and women. But today, it is much easier to print a periodical magazine such as The Heartbeat of the Remnant. We simply take up the pen or keyboard and write. Our document is then digitally edited and electronically sent to the printer. After the files are uploaded, the printing press will print 6,000 copies in a little over 12 hours. It is then finished and mailed to 51 countries around the world and many states in the U.S. Printing has come a long way since 1436 when each page had to be set up and printed individually.

According to a 2010 Google project, just under 130 million books were published globally. Since then, UNESCO estimates that approximately 2.2 million new titles are published each year. By adding these yearly publications to the initial count, we can estimate that as of 2024, there are more than 160 million unique books in the world. This number does not account for books that may have gone out of print or been discontinued since their initial publication. The wise preacher was right when he wrote, “And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecclesiastes 12:12).

Let’s use this freedom of the press to God’s glory while we have the chance. I work for Christian Aid Ministries, and we regularly hear testimonies from Christians in closed and restricted countries who are extremely blessed to receive Christian literature. One person from an undisclosed location wrote, “. . . we all take turns reading the magazine in church. A very edifying magazine. God bless you! God’s blessings.” Hearing testimonies like this makes me more thankful for what we have. But I’m sure people in persecuted countries value their Christian literature more highly than we who have Bibles and Christian literature in abundance.

In this issue, we reprinted two articles by request. A Glorious Church by Barry Grant and Joy in the Crevices by Sheryl Zeiset were both first printed in 2019. May our churches demonstrate the virtues and our homes radiate the beauty that is portrayed in these timeless articles.

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin

Tarehe 21 Januari, 1525, ilikuwa kumbukumbu ya miaka 500 ya Anabaptism. Miaka mia tano iliyopita, tukio kubwa katika historia ya kanisa la Kikristo lilitokea. Kikundi kidogo cha Wakristo wa msimamo mkali kilikusanyika kwa utulivu katika nyumba ya Felix Mantz huko Zürich, Uswisi. Serikali ya kanisa la mji wa Zürich ilikuwa imewaamuru wazazi kuwabaptiza watoto wao wa vichanga au kukumbwa na adhabu ya kuachwa nyumbani. Kukusanyika pamoja kwa ajili ya masomo ya Maandiko na vikao vya sala pia kulikuwa kinyume cha sheria. Hata hivyo, kwenye jioni hiyo ya baridi yenye umuhimu, Feliz Mantz, Conrad Grebel, George Blaurock, na wengine wachache walifanya utii wao hatua moja zaidi. Baada ya kuomba na kujitolea kumtumikia Mungu kwa uaminifu, George Blaurock aliomba Conrad Grebel amkubatishe kwa imani halisi ya Kikristo, jambo ambalo Conrad alilitenda. Wengine pia waliomba ubatizo, na George, kwa mzunguko, aliwabatiza pia. Na hivyo basi, Anabaptism, kama tunavyoijua, ilizaliwa.

Ingawa hawa wanaume watatu walikuwa sehemu muhimu katika historia ya Anabaptist, Mageuzi hayakuanza nao. Kile kilichochochea moto wa kuhuishwa kilianzishwa miaka 88 kabla yake. Mnamo 1436, fundi dhahabu Mjerumani aitwaye Johannes Gutenberg alibuni mashine ya kuchapisha yenye herufi zinazoweza kuhamishwa. Hii iliibua mabadiliko makubwa katika uchapishaji, na vitabu vilikuwa vinachapishwa kwa wingi zaidi. Badala ya vitabu vya wachache tu mikononi mwa matajiri, sasa mtu wa kawaida angeweza kununua vitabu. Vitabu vya kwanza kuchapishwa kwa mashine ya Gutenberg vilikuwa Maandiko. Watu wa kawaida walipoanza kununua na kusoma Maandiko, walianza kutambua kwamba giza la ukandamizaji wa kidini lilikuwa linawazuia kuelewa nuru ya kweli ya Neno la Mungu. Na hivyo, Mageuzi yalizaliwa.

Ruka kwa haraka miaka 588. Karatasi iliyochapishwa bado inahamasisha wanaume na wanawake. Lakini leo, ni rahisi zaidi kuchapisha jarida kama The Heartbeat of the Remnant. Tunachofanya ni kuchukua kalamu au kibodi na kuandika. Hati yetu kisha huhaririwa kidijitali na kutumwa kwa njia ya kielektroniki kwa mchapishaji. Baada ya mafaili kupakiwa, mashine ya kuchapisha itachapisha nakala 6,000 ndani ya takriban saa 12. Kisha inakamilika na kutumwa kwa posta katika nchi 51 kote ulimwenguni na mikoa mingi nchini Marekani. Uchapishaji umepiga hatua kubwa tangu 1436 wakati kila ukurasa ilikuwa inatakiwa kupangwa na kuchapishwa kando kwa kando.

Kulingana na mradi wa Google wa 2010, takriban vitabu milioni 130 vilichapishwa duniani kote. Tangu wakati huo, UNESCO inakadiria kuwa takriban vichwa vipya milioni 2.2 vinachapishwa kila mwaka. Kwa kuongeza machapisho haya ya kila mwaka kwenye hesabu ya awali, tunaweza kukadiria kuwa hadi mwaka 2024, kuna zaidi ya vitabu milioni 160 vya kipekee duniani. Idadi hii haizingatii vitabu ambavyo huenda vimeachwa kuchapishwa tena au kutoweka tangu machapisho yao ya awali. Mhubiri mwenye busara alikuwa sahihi alipyoandika, “Zaidi ya hayo, mwanangu, kaeni ukumbushwe; kwa kuwa kuunda vitabu vingi hakuna mwisho, na bidii ya kujifunza ni uchovu wa mwili” (Mhubiri 12:12).

Tumie uhuru huu wa vyombo vya habari kwa utukufu wa Mungu wakati tuna nafasi. Mimi nafanya kazi kwa Christian Aid Ministries, na mara kwa mara tunasikia ushuhuda kutoka kwa Wakristo katika nchi zilizofungwa na zilizo na vikwazo ambao wanabarikiwa sana kupokea fasihi ya Kikristo. Mtu mmoja kutoka mahali pasipyoelezwa aliandika, “. . . sote tunageuza kusoma jarida kanisani. Jarida lenye kunyoosha moyo. Mungu awabariki! Baraka za Mungu.” Kusikia mashuhuda kama haya kunanifanya nimshukuru Mungu zaidi kwa kile tulicho nacho. Lakini nina hakika watu katika nchi zinazodhulumiwa wanathamini fasihi yao ya Kikristo zaidi kuliko sisi wenye Biblia na fasihi ya Kikristo kwa wingi.

Baraka kwa wote,

Edward Martin

And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter (John 10:22).

As the maddening winds howl about him, man turns his collar to the cold and damp. Little praise arises for the season that greets him at his weakest point and seeks to discomfort and discourage him from the zest of life. Winter settles in as a formidable authority and arouses anxiety not so much by the infliction of pain but the removal of the pleasant. As we cross the equinox, “the days get longer, and winter gets stronger”, states the old proverb, and it remains incisively correct.

Winter is the season of profound, persistent cold that drives the frost deeper and thickens the ice on the ponds. Man and beast battle its ferocity, and even the lifeless machinery rebels against winter’s adamant arrival. Chilly drafts penetrate every crack and crevice, forcing their heartless presence into the most private chambers. As the woodpiles shrink, utility bills increase in the struggle to resist winter’s array of armed forces. While a few gay tunes, such as Winter Wonderland, seek to capitalize upon its majestic moments, winter is generally despised by the normal inhabitants of this earth. We grimace under the menacing icy grip that holds us captive and longingly anticipate its eventual release.

Spring may have its equal share of soggy and uncomfortable appointments and ragged days. Northern tradition states that the robins must get snowed on three times before the full arrival of spring. But springtime is never void of the hope and glory of better days ahead. Summer can be unbearable with its burning heat and humidity, but it bears a semblance of blessed fruitfulness on every side, and few will slow their activities to notice its discomforts. The autumn days carry their nostalgic enchantment while the beauty of nature is painted in the most remarkable colors on the foliage of the landscape. The bounties of harvest provide an aura of rejoicing in their sheaves, and man’s heart is still merry with the prospects of maturing life. And then comes . . .

Winter

Our Lord experienced the fullness of it; probably not the fullness of the natural elements that those of us in the northern climates face, but the season of apparent fruitlessness. Some said, “He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” (John 10:20). At a time when there was to be a feast of dedication, “it was winter.” There was a massive division among the people. Confusion reigned on every side. Jesus had just healed a blind man, and the Jews cast him out of the temple. Such fruitless and cold stony hearts inhabited the fields that were acclaimed to be “white unto harvest.” The icy grips of sin had hardened the hearts of humanity, and the meadows of religion were littered with barren stalks draped with the remains of empty husks. The beloved disciple wasted no words when he brought us the fact that . . . it was winter.

“Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter” (Psalm 74:17).

It is easy to believe that God has created summertime. The tunes on a perfect summer day sing to us of the Divine. The beauty revolving about us everywhere speaks of His presence. The cheering birds in every tree, the warmth of the pleasant sunshine, and the amazing prodigy of life draw our hearts to the Giver by a thousand invisible filaments of life. These all testify to the truth that “Thou hast made summer.”

The days of winter are different. “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). We share similar sentiments to those of Nathaniel toward the winter months, for it is not so easy to see the hand of God there. There is a great deal of suffering and rejection that we feel penetrating our inner man. I obviously speak not to the season within nature but to the seasons of life that parallel its existence. We do well to aid our frail faith by some solid affirmation that God has made winter, as well, and that we ought not to doubt His divine purposes in it. What, but a season of chilling despair and discomfort can arouse our apathetic souls to . . .

Appreciation

Absence makes the heart grow fonder. Thus does the advent of winter incite our appreciation for summer. We would be blind if summer were perpetually present. It has been aptly said that our dear ones are only ours when we have lost them. When the winter season finally claims their last breath, we then begin to appreciate them for who they really were. It is not the man with an abundance of uninterrupted health who feels most deeply the value of his well-being. That realization arrives on his doorstep the day his health is shattered. There have been many wealthy men who had previously known the stark bareness of bankruptcy. This indelibly embossed a permanent mark in their character that fitted them for the success that followed in its wake.

So the Christian will often experience a season of winter—a time when all that he had labored over, longed for and loved lies languishing beneath the mounds of sterile hopeless drifts. John the Baptist prophesied boldly while the vision was fresh and the crowds pressed around to hear him preach. But the dark and cold prison cell was difficult for him to appreciate. Yet, God has made winter, and these seasons in our lives are paramount to our spiritual well-being.

Strengthening

In the 1700s, a luthier by the name of Stradivari created violins unequaled in their excellence for beautiful sound. As modern experts puzzled long over their inability to create a similar instrument, most have resolved that the wood of the day had been seasoned by difficult winters, producing a quality that cannot be replicated in our day. All nature strains under the duress of the winter months, and man is not exempt. The short days and deep, brazen chill of the night apply a great demand upon our will. In summer, it is comparatively easy to get out of bed at the appointed hour. The earth is warm, the birds are busy singing, and the light is streaming through the open windows. But in the dark of a frigid winter morning, to fling back the covers and arise in a triumphant air is a challenging proposition. It demands a solid resolution to achieve and makes a failure out of many good intentions.

As we broaden that thought to encompass the soul of man, we reach a truth that cannot be denied. Those who have borne the deep burdens of hard living have an innate strength ingrained in their character that those of a mild environment cannot apprehend. The moral character of Adonijah had eroded, for “his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?” (1 Kings 1:6). This is the bane of easy living. Those who will insulate themselves on every side from the buffeting of winter will, no doubt, incur a weakening of the will. Those who can conquer their will in the presence of a blatantly cold society are on the highway to success. Summer is languid; but winter makes us resolute. We need to do things even when we don’t feel like doing them. And thus, God has made the winter.

Togetherness

“If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?” (Ecc. 4:11). There is no need for such togetherness in the summer—and no desire for it either. The crackling stove has a mesmerizing effect upon the household members and most of our winter evening activities center around it. We speak in the same breath, of hearth and home, and it is in winter that the hearth glows and love grows.

There are but shallow relationships among those who have known no hardship. It takes the heavy austerity of winter to perform the genius of love in our hearts. Adversity levels the playing field, while sage and simpleton pull together in the same yoke. Often, as death wraps its cold fingers around a frail body, loved ones rush to the bedside. Past grievances are forgotten in the solemnity of the moment. It was at the gates of winter that “Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age” (Genesis 25:8). It is here that the separating curtains of the long-standing conflict between Isaac and Ishmael abated and a joint effort between the two brothers “buried him in the cave of Machpelah”.

While none of us shall ever hope for the political unrest that would bring persecution and the removal of religious freedom from our land, it is still my belief that our carnal church divisions will cease upon its advent. It takes winter to pull us together, and Christ was the vehicle upon whom it rode in. “It was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch” (John 10:23). There, before the inauguration of His death, His disciples were all pushing for the head of the line and striving to be the greatest. Now, after the cold harsh removal of the green tree, they were all found to be “with one accord in Solomon’s porch” (Acts 5:12). Such is the ministry of winter that our God has gifted us with.

Sympathy

For some reason, it seems that we must receive a full dosage of maltreatment before the door of our hearts is unlocked to thoughts of the sorrowful plight of others. One can only wonder what the Good Samaritan must have experienced to be so thoroughly moved by the scene of the man in the ditch. Did not the Jews paint a fresh emblem of hatred and disdain before him on the canvas of each new day? For some, the ill-treatment has a tendency to harden the heart. These go through life in reclusive fashion, with bitterness and spite at the helm of their ship. Any acquaintances that remotely fail their discrimination are categorized as suspect, and avoided.

There are others who have endured the cold blast of winter and loathe that any should have to experience the same. These hearts are quickly aroused to pity and carry bias sympathy toward those of similar plight. Even the rich man who met his wintry death and was now in eternal hell was moved to extend mercy to his five brethren who were bound for the same dreadful destination. How much more should our sluggish hearts stir to charity when met with such discomforts as spiritual winter? Can we greet our fellow man with the same stern, icy glare that has smitten us in the face in bygone days? Is there no storehouse of mercy to extend to the wayward soul who is reaping the cold reality of his folly-filled life that he has sown in his youth?

It was winter in the days when our Lord walked in the temple, and surely, the spiritual environment today is no less frigid. “Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Matthew 24:12). Those of us who choose to despise this barren wilderness can live reclusive at our will. The rest of us shall readily acknowledge that our God hast made . . . winter and allow it to have its perfecting work in our hearts.

Og det var i Jerusalem høytiden for innvielsen, og det var vinter (Johannes 10:22).

Mens de rasende vindene uler omkring ham, vender mennesket kragen opp mot kulden og fuktigheten. Lite lovsang stiger for årstiden som møter ham på hans svakeste punkt og søker å berøre ham med ubehag og frata ham livslysten. Vinteren slår seg ned som en formidabel myndighet og vekker angst ikke så mye ved å påføre smerte som ved å fjerne det behagelige. Når vi passerer jevndøgn, «dagene blir lengre, og vinteren blir kraftigere», sier det gamle ordtaket, og det står fortsatt skarpt riktig.

Vinteren er årstiden for dyp, vedvarende kulde som driver frosten dypere og gjør isen på dammene tykkere. Menneske og dyr kjemper mot dens villskap, og selv livløse maskiner protesterer mot vinterens ubøyelige ankomst. Kalde trekk trenger gjennom hver sprekk og krinkel og tvinger sin nådeløse tilstedeværelse inn i de mest private gemakker. Mens vedstabelen minkes, stiger strømregningene i kampen for å stå imot vinterens oppbud av væpnede krefter. Mens noen muntre melodier, som Winter Wonderland, forsøker å utnytte dens majestetiske øyeblikk, foraktet vinteren vanligvis av jordens vanlige innbyggere. Vi grimaserer under det truende, iskalde grepet som holder oss fanget, og venter lengselsfullt på dens endelige løslatelse.

Våren kan ha sin del av sølete og ubehagelige dager og rufsete stunder. Nordlig tradisjon sier at rødstruper må bli snødd på tre ganger før våren er fullt ankommet. Men våren er aldri uten håpet og herligheten over bedre dager som kommer. Sommeren kan være ubærlig med sin brennende varme og fuktighet, men den bærer et preg av velsignet fruktbarhet på alle kanter, og få vil sakke tempoet for å merke dens ubehag. Høstdagene bærer sin nostalgiske sjarm mens naturens skjønnhet males i de mest bemerkelsesverdige fargene på landskapets løvverk. Høstens gaver gir en aura av fryd i sine neg, og menneskets hjerte er fortsatt lystelig ved utsiktene til modnende liv. Og så kommer . . .

Vinter

Vår Herre erfarte dens fylde; sannsynligvis ikke fylden av de naturkrefter som vi i nordlige klima møter, men årstiden for tilsynelatende fruktbarhetens fravær. Noen sa: «Han har en dæmon, og han er gal; hvorfor hører dere på ham?» (Johannes 10:20). På et tidspunkt da det skulle være en innvielsesfest, «var det vinter.» Det var en massiv splittelse blant folket. Forvirring rådet på alle kanter. Jesus hadde nettopp helbredet en blind mann, og jødene kastet ham ut av templet. Slike fruktløse og kalde, steinharde hjerter befolket åkrene som ble erklært å være «hvite til høst» (Johannes 4:35). Syndens iskalde grep hadde herdet menneskehjertene, og religiøse enger var strødd med nakne stengler dekket av rester av tomme skrel. Den elskede disippel sløste ingen ord da han gav oss faktumet at . . . det var vinter.

«Du har satt alle jordens grenser; du har gjort sommer og vinter» (Salme 74:17).

Det er lett å tro at Gud har skapt sommeren. Melodiene på en perfekt sommerdag synger om det Guddommelige for oss. Skjønnheten som omgir oss overalt taler om Hans nærvær. De muntre fuglene i hvert tre, varmen fra den behagelige solskinnet, og det forbløffende under av liv trekker våre hjerter til Giveren med tusen usynlige livsfilamenter. Alt dette vitner om sannheten at «Du har gjort sommeren.»

Vintrene er annerledes. «Kan det komme noe godt fra Nasaret?» (Johannes 1:46). Vi deler Nathanaels lignende følelser over vintermånedene, for det er ikke så lett å se Guds hånd der. Det er mye lidelse og avvisning som vi føler gjennomtrenger vårt indre menneske. Jeg taler åpenbart ikke om årstiden i naturen, men om livets årstider som paralleller dens tilværelse. Vi gjør klokt i å styrke vår svake tro med en solid bekreftelse på at Gud også har gjort vinter, og at vi ikke bør tvile på Hans guddommelige formål i den. Hva annet enn en sesong av isende fortvilelse og ubehag kan vekke våre apatiske sjeler til . . .

Takknemlighet

Fravær gjør hjertet mer kjært. Slik vekker vinterens komme vår takknemlighet for sommeren. Vi ville vært blinde om sommeren var til stede uten opphold. Det er blitt treffende sagt at våre kjære kun er våre når vi har mistet dem. Når vintersesongen endelig krever deres siste åndedrag, begynner vi da å verdsette dem for hvem de virkelig var. Det er ikke mannen med overflod av uavbrutt helse som kjenner størst dybde i sin velværes verdi. Den erkjennelsen banker på hans dør den dagen helsen blir knust. Det har vært mange velstående menn som tidligere hadde kjent den barske nakenheten av konkurs. Dette preget uutslettelig og etterlot et varig merke i deres karakter som rustet dem for den suksessen som fulgte i kjølvannet.

Slik vil den kristne ofte oppleve en vintersesong—en tid når alt han hadde arbeidet for, lengtet etter og elsket ligger hen under hauger av sterile, håpløse snøføyker. Johannes Døperen profeterte modig mens visjonen var fersk og folkemengdene trengte seg rundt for å høre ham preke. Men den mørke og kalde fengselscellen var vanskelig for ham å verdsette. Likevel, Gud har gjort vinter, og disse sesongene i våre liv er avgjørende for vår åndelige velvære.

Styrkende

I 1700-årene skapte en lutbygger ved navn Stradivari fioliner uten sidestykke i sin utmerkelse for vakker klang. Mens moderne eksperter lenge undret seg over sin manglende evne til å lage et lignende instrument, har de fleste besunnet seg at tidens tre var herdet av vanskelige vintre, og produserte en kvalitet som ikke kan gjenskapes i vår tid. Hele naturen strever under vintermånedenes påkjenning, og mennesket er ikke unntatt. De korte dagene og den dype, rå kulden i natten legger et stort krav på vår vilje. Om sommeren er det forholdsvis lett å stå opp til fastsatt tid. Jorden er varm, fuglene synger travelt, og lyset strømmer gjennom de åpne vinduene. Men i mørket på en isende vintermorgen, å kaste dynen til side og stige opp med triumferende mot er en utfordrende forestilling. Det krever en solid besluttsomhet å gjennomføre og gjør mange gode intensjoner til nederlag.

Når vi utvider den tanken til å omfatte menneskesjelen, når vi en sannhet som ikke kan fornektes. De som har båret de dype byrdene av et hardt liv har en medfødt styrke inngravert i sin karakter som de fra et mildere miljø ikke kan fatte. Adonijas moralske karakter hadde erodert, for «hans far hadde ikke irettesatt ham når som helst og sagt: Hvorfor har du gjort slik?» (1 Kongebok 1:6). Dette er forbannelsen over lettvint liv. De som isolerer seg på alle sider fra vinterens kast mister uten tvil styrken i viljen. De som kan overvinne sin vilje i møte med et åpenbart kaldt samfunn, er på veien til suksess. Sommeren er slapp; men vinteren gjør oss beslutsomme. Vi trenger å gjøre ting selv når vi ikke har lyst til det. Og således, Gud har gjort vinteren.

Sammenhet

«Om to ligger sammen, blir de varme; men hvordan kan én bli varm alene?» (Forkynneren 4:11). Slik sammenhet er ikke nødvendig om sommeren—og heller ikke ønsket. Den knitrende ovnen har en fortryllende effekt på husets medlemmer, og de fleste av våre vinterkveldsaktiviteter dreier seg rundt den. Vi snakker i samme ånd om ildsted og hjem, og det er i vinteren at ildstedet gløder og kjærligheten vokser.

Det finnes bare overfladiske relasjoner blant dem som ikke har kjent nød. Det krever vinterens tunge strenghet å fremkalle kjærlighetens geni i våre hjerter. Motgang jevner spillefeltet, mens klok og enfoldig trekker sammen i samme oksebyrde. Ofte, når døden legger sine kalde fingre rundt en skrøpelig kropp, skynder de kjære seg til sykesengen. Tidligere fornærmelser glemmes i øyeblikkets høytid. Det var ved vinterens porter at «Abraham gav opp ånden, og døde i en god alder» (1 Mosebok 25:8). Det er her de skilende gardinene fra langvarig strid mellom Isak og Ismael stilnet, og en felles innsats mellom de to brødrene «begravet ham i Makpelas hule».

Selv om ingen av oss noen gang bør ønske den politiske uro som ville bringe forfølgelse og frata oss religiøs frihet, er det fortsatt min tro at våre kjødelige kirkedelingers stridigheter vil opphøre ved dens inntog. Det krever vinter for å samle oss, og Kristus var kjøretøyet det red på. «Det var vinter. Og Jesus vandret i templet i Salomos søylegang» (Johannes 10:23). Der, før innledningen til Hans død, presset disiplene alle for å være fremst i rekken og strove om å være størst. Nå, etter det kalde, harde bruddet med det grønne tre, ble de alle funnet å være «enkelt i ett sinn i Salomos søylegang» (Apostlenes gjerninger 5:12). Slik er vinterens tjeneste som vår Gud har gitt oss.

Medfølelse

Av en eller annen grunn synes det som om vi må motta en full dose av mishandling før hjertets dør låses opp for tankene på andres sørgelige kår. Man kan bare undre seg over hva Den barmhjertige samaritanen må ha erfart for å bli så grundig beveget av synet av mannen i grøfta. Malte ikke jødene et friskt emblem av hat og forakt foran ham på hver nye dags lerret? For noen har dårlig behandling en tendens til å herde hjertet. Disse går gjennom livet i tilbaketrukkethet, med bitterhet og nag ved roret. Enhver bekjent som på en eller annen måte faller utenfor deres diskriminering blir kategorisert som mistenkelig og unngått.

Det finnes andre som har utholdt vinterens kalde støt og avskyr at noen må oppleve det samme. Disse hjerter vekkes raskt til medlidenhet og bærer en partisk sympati overfor dem som deler lignende kår. Selv den rike mannen som møtte sin vintrige død og nå var i evig helvete, ble beveget til å utvide barmhjertighet til sine fem brødre som var på vei mot samme fryktelige skjebne. Hvor mye mer bør ikke våre sløve hjerter røres til veldedighet når vi møter slike ubehag som åndelig vinter? Kan vi møte vår neste med samme strenge, iskalde blikk som har slått oss i ansiktet i fordums dager? Finnes det ingen forrådskammer av barmhjertighet å strekke ut til den vankelmodige sjel som høster den kalde realiteten av sitt ungdommelig sådde dårskap?

Det var vinter i de dager da vår Herre vandret i templet, og sikkert er den åndelige atmosfæren i dag ikke mindre isende. «Fordi lovløsheten skal bli mange, skal kjærligheten hos de fleste bli kald» (Matteus 24:12). De av oss som velger å forakte denne golde villmark kan leve tilbaketrukket etter eget ønske. Resten av oss vil lett erkjenne at vår Gud har gjort . . . vinter og la den få sitt fullendende verk i våre hjerter.

The people we commonly refer to as the Russian Mennonites came into being as a group in a way quite similar to that of us with an Anabaptist heritage. We sprang from the same areas of Europe, from much of the same teachings of early Anabaptism, and have both experienced many of the same temptations and pitfalls, though at different times and locations.

This article will not focus on the beginnings of the Russian Mennonites apart from a brief overview. The group first entered Russia upon the urgings of the Viceroy Potemkin, who came into authority over the area now known as Ukraine after its annexation by Russia in 1783. The area had been under his partial administration since 1774, and he was eager to populate the land with foreign settlers. The residents of New Russia, as it was then called, were mostly nomads and Cossacks, a seminomadic group present in the steppes of Russia. The Mennonites in Danzig, Poland, were first approached with the offer of land, which would have appealed to them because they were routinely denied land ownership as a semi-persecuted people at that time. This offer came in August of 1786, and two brothers from the Danzig church were sent to survey the land and make arrangements for possible immigration.

The first immigration of 462 families began in 1788, and the “Old Colony” was established at Chortitza. They were afforded freedom of religion, exemption from military service, and the right to maintain their own schools and governances.

The Mennonites thrived in their new homeland. Although the first years were hard, partially due to the fact that mostly poorer families and those not in church leadership chose to resettle in Russia, the group soon began to transform the barren plains and steppes into rich agricultural communities. As the churches grew, so did their prosperity.

This period of relative peace lasted for over a century, until the late 1800s, when the Russian government, dissatisfied with the number of foreign settlements inside its borders, began applying pressure to many of the groups it had invited to settle its land some 100 years before. The Mennonites were not the only ones targeted, as many groups from various nations had established themselves in Russia. Steps taken against the Mennonites included pressure to participate in the armed forces as well as pressure to drop the German language that the communities had been using in favor of the Russian language. As these pressures increased, some Mennonites chose to flee the country in the 1870s. The majority, however, by now quite wealthy and affluent in comparison to their Russian peasant neighbors, chose to stay and weather the storm.

Unbeknownst to them, a full-scale revolution that would reshape Russia as a country was just around the corner. In 1917, the Bolsheviks came to power through the October Revolution, an event where the reigning tsar, or emperor, was deposed and exiled, and a new government was set up. A civil war broke out, and much of the fighting raged over the lands occupied by the Mennonites. Here, it is necessary to insert a brief history of the ideology of this new government.

The October Revolution and its subsequent change in government were fueled by a class war. As opposed to Nazi Germany, where a person could be arrested and killed for their race, in Russia, a person could and would be arrested for their class, for example, property ownership was seen as a crime against the people, and so the wealthier class of Russian peasants and farmers, those who most often owned property and employed the lower class of peasants, became an instant target a revolution that claimed to want to distribute all property and resources evenly amongst its citizenry.

By this time, the strong agricultural society of the Mennonites had transformed Ukraine into a breadbasket, its vast fields sown with wheat developed specifically by the Mennonites: Turkey Red Wheat. This hardy crop had made the Mennonite church quite wealthy, and their colonies had grown and flourished into villages of comfort and, at times, extravagance. This must have been a two-fold insult to the still impoverished peasants of Russia. Not only was there a large group of people in their midst that taught, spoke, and did their dealings in a language not of the Motherland, but these people also were wealthy beyond most peasants’ dreams.

It is, therefore, no surprise that when the kulaks, the wealthy class of peasants, came under persecution from the new government, the Mennonites were seen as the enemy of the people. As the civil war raged over Mennonite lands, villages were burnt and decimated, people executed or driven off, and livestock and grain plundered. Eventually, this period of fighting did come to an end, but for those few who survived the destruction, there was no reprieve to be found.

With the label of kulak and being generally defenseless, the Mennonites faced intense persecution. Religious services were rarely allowed, and the agricultural communities that had fed Russia and many others besides were collectivized and put under government control. Many of their churches ceased to exist entirely, although those in the east tended to last longer than the western villages.

Imagine then, to a people accustomed for generations to the favor and benevolence of material possessions and success, that all things material are stripped away. In a historical eye blink, the wealthy become the poor, and the favored become the hated. Even with a strong Christian faith, such a turn of events would shock and confuse.

But further tests were yet ahead for those who endured the first 25 years of the Soviet persecution. With the memory of their easy lives still fresh, the dawn of World War II brought a unique and enticing opportunity: the rise of a government that promoted the well-being of the German race, that valued those groups that could turn an empty prairie into a sprawling farm, that was vehemently anti-Communist- to this beleaguered group of believers, this must have seemed to be a God sent miracle to deliver them from their burdensome exile.

And so, they embraced the invading Germans. We readers, who are blessed with the ability to see the end result of these people’s decisions, can certainly make a good guess at what the end result was of wholesale support for the Nazis, but we must remember the scenarios that these Mennonites found themselves in...it was not one that would have been easy to decipher and decide upon if it were to be judged by man’s knowledge.

And so it was that the descendants of those helpless believers who gave their bodies at the stake and sword aligned themselves with a worldly kingdom that promised to protect and provide for them. In exchange for an eternal heritage, they chose to hope that the might of the German army would win back their earthly heritage and riches, and it was in this might that they trusted, forming bands of men who fought alongside the Germans against their old neighbors.

History did not deviate from its course, and the German army was eventually beaten back to its own borders and then further, and yet further into German lands. Before this retreating army ran those that had looked to it for their deliverance.

The atrocities of the Soviet government against its citizens are well documented in various works, most famously in the Gulag Archipelago, a book written by a Russian officer who was accused of treason. That author, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, painted a terrible picture of the treatment and exile of those who had opposed the USSR. Amongst the imprisoned or executed millions described in his tomes, there lie the remnants of a people who began as we did, experienced the smile of prosperity as we do, and then, treasuring that prosperity, lost it in calamitous fashion. We would do well to consider the paths we choose, as the wise king of the Scriptures instructs us, lest we, too, fall in the pursuit of prosperity. “Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established” (Proverbs 4:26).

O povo a que comumente nos referimos como menonitas russos tornou-se um grupo de forma bastante semelhante à nossa herança anabatista. Surgimos das mesmas áreas da Europa, de grande parte dos mesmos ensinamentos do anabatismo primitivo, e ambos experimentamos muitas das mesmas tentações e armadilhas, embora em épocas e lugares diferentes.

Este artigo não se concentrará nos primórdios dos menonitas russos, exceto por uma breve visão geral. O grupo entrou pela primeira vez na Rússia por incentivo do vice-rei Potemkin, que passou a ter autoridade sobre a área agora conhecida como Ucrânia após sua anexação pela Rússia em 1783. A região estava sob sua administração parcial desde 1774, e ele estava ansioso para povoar a terra com colonos estrangeiros. Os residentes da Nova Rússia, como então se chamava, eram em sua maioria nômades e cossacos, um grupo seminômade presente nas estepes da Rússia. Os menonitas em Danzig, Polônia, foram os primeiros a receber a oferta de terras, o que teria lhes agradado porque rotineiramente lhes era negada a propriedade da terra como um povo semi-perseguido naquela época. Essa oferta veio em agosto de 1786, e dois irmãos da igreja de Danzig foram enviados para sondar a terra e fazer arranjos para uma possível imigração.

A primeira imigração de 462 famílias começou em 1788, e a “Colônia Antiga” foi estabelecida em Chortitza. Foi-lhes concedida liberdade religiosa, isenção do serviço militar e o direito de manter suas próprias escolas e governanças.

Os menonitas prosperaram em sua nova pátria. Embora os primeiros anos tenham sido duros, em parte pelo fato de que em sua maioria famílias mais pobres e aqueles que não ocupavam a liderança da igreja escolheram reassentar-se na Rússia, o grupo logo começou a transformar as planícies e estepes áridas em ricas comunidades agrícolas. À medida que as igrejas cresciam, crescia também sua prosperidade.

Esse período de relativa paz durou por mais de um século, até o final do século XIX, quando o governo russo, insatisfeito com o número de assentamentos estrangeiros dentro de suas fronteiras, começou a aplicar pressão a muitos dos grupos que havia convidado para povoar suas terras cerca de 100 anos antes. Os menonitas não foram os únicos alvos, pois muitos grupos de várias nações haviam se estabelecido na Rússia. Medidas tomadas contra os menonitas incluíram pressão para participar das forças armadas, bem como pressão para abandonar a língua alemã que as comunidades vinham usando em favor da língua russa. À medida que essas pressões aumentaram, alguns menonitas escolheram fugir do país na década de 1870. A maioria, porém, já bastante rica e afluente em comparação com seus vizinhos camponeses russos, optou por ficar e enfrentar a tempestade.

Sem que o soubessem, uma revolução em larga escala que remodelaria a Rússia como país estava próxima. Em 1917, os bolcheviques chegaram ao poder por meio da Revolução de Outubro, um evento em que o czar reinante, ou imperador, foi deposto e exilado, e um novo governo foi estabelecido. Uma guerra civil irrompeu, e grande parte dos combates ocorreu nas terras ocupadas pelos menonitas. Aqui, é necessário inserir um breve histórico da ideologia desse novo governo.

A Revolução de Outubro e sua subsequente mudança de governo foram alimentadas por uma guerra de classes. Ao contrário da Alemanha nazista, onde uma pessoa podia ser presa e morta por sua raça, na Rússia uma pessoa podia e seria presa por sua classe; por exemplo, a posse de propriedade era vista como um crime contra o povo, e assim a classe mais rica de camponeses e agricultores russos, aqueles que mais frequentemente possuíam propriedades e empregavam a classe camponesa mais baixa, tornou-se alvo instantâneo de uma revolução que afirmava querer distribuir toda propriedade e recursos de forma igual entre seus cidadãos.

Naquela época, a forte sociedade agrícola dos menonitas havia transformado a Ucrânia em um celeiro, seus vastos campos semeados com um trigo desenvolvido especificamente pelos menonitas: o Trigo Turkey Red. Essa cultura resistente tornara a igreja menonita bastante rica, e suas colônias haviam crescido e florescido em vilarejos de conforto e, por vezes, extravagância. Isso deve ter sido uma ofensa dupla para os camponeses ainda empobrecidos da Rússia. Não só havia um grande grupo de pessoas em seu meio que ensinava, falava e fazia negócios em uma língua não pertencente à Pátria, mas essas pessoas também eram ricas além dos sonhos da maioria dos camponeses.

Não é, portanto, surpresa que quando os kulaks, a classe camponesa mais rica, passaram a ser perseguidos pelo novo governo, os menonitas fossem vistos como inimigos do povo. Enquanto a guerra civil devastava as terras menonitas, vilas foram queimadas e dizimadas, pessoas executadas ou expulsas, e o gado e o grão saqueados. Eventualmente, esse período de combates chegou ao fim, mas para aqueles poucos que sobreviveram à destruição, não havia descanso a ser encontrado.

Com o rótulo de kulak e sendo geralmente indefesos, os menonitas enfrentaram intensa perseguição. Os cultos religiosos raramente eram permitidos, e as comunidades agrícolas que haviam alimentado a Rússia e muitos outros foram coletivizadas e colocadas sob controle governamental. Muitas de suas igrejas deixaram de existir completamente, embora as do leste tendessem a durar mais que as vilas do oeste.

Imagine então, para um povo acostumado por gerações ao favor e à benevolência das posses materiais e do sucesso, que todas as coisas materiais lhes sejam tiradas. Num piscar de olhos históricos, os ricos tornam-se pobres, e os favorecidos tornam-se odiados. Mesmo com uma fé cristã vigorosa, tal reviravolta de acontecimentos chocaria e confundiria.

Mas testes adicionais ainda aguardavam aqueles que suportaram os primeiros 25 anos de perseguição soviética. Com a memória de suas vidas fáceis ainda fresca, a aurora da Segunda Guerra Mundial trouxe uma oportunidade única e sedutora: a ascensão de um governo que promovia o bem-estar da raça alemã, que valorizava aqueles grupos que podiam transformar uma pradaria vazia em uma fazenda vasta, que era veementemente anti-comunista — para esse grupo sofredor de crentes, isso devia parecer um milagre enviado por Deus para livrá-los do exílio penoso.

E assim, abraçaram os alemães invasores. Nós, leitores, que temos a bênção de ver o resultado final das decisões desse povo, certamente podemos fazer uma boa suposição sobre qual foi o desfecho do apoio maciço aos nazistas, mas devemos lembrar os cenários em que esses menonitas se encontraram... não era uma situação que tivesse sido fácil decifrar e decidir, se fosse julgada pelo conhecimento humano.

E assim foi que os descendentes daqueles crentes desamparados que deram seus corpos na estaca e na espada alinharam-se com um reino mundano que prometia protegê-los e provê-los. Em troca de uma herança eterna, escolheram esperar que o poder do exército alemão reconquistasse sua herança terrena e suas riquezas, e foi nesse poder que confiaram, formando bandos de homens que lutaram ao lado dos alemães contra seus antigos vizinhos.

A história não se desviou de seu curso, e o exército alemão foi eventualmente repelido para suas próprias fronteiras e, depois, mais adentro das terras alemãs. Antes dessa retirada, fugiram aqueles que nele haviam confiado para sua libertação.

As atrocidades do governo soviético contra seus cidadãos estão bem documentadas em várias obras, mais famoso em O Arquipélago Gulag, um livro escrito por um autor russo acusado de traição. Aquele autor, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, pintou um quadro terrível do tratamento e do exílio daqueles que se opuseram à URSS. Entre os milhões presos ou executados descritos em seus tomos, encontram-se os remanescentes de um povo que começou como nós, experimentou o sorriso da prosperidade como nós, e então, estimando essa prosperidade, a perdeu de forma calamidosa. Faríamos bem em considerar os caminhos que escolhemos, como o sábio rei das Escrituras nos instrui, para que nós também não caiamos na busca da prosperidade. “Considera o caminho dos teus pés, e que todos os teus caminhos sejam bem estabelecidos” (Provérbios 4:26).

City of God, how broad and far
outspread thy walls sublime!
The true thy chartered freemen are
of every age and clime:

One holy church, one army strong,
one steadfast, high intent;
one working band, one harvest-song,
one King omnipotent.

How purely hath thy speech come down
from man's primaeval youth!
How grandly hath thine empire grown
of freedom, love, and truth!

How gleam thy watch-fires through the night
with never-fainting ray!
How rise thy towers, serene and bright,
to meet the dawning day!

In vain the surge's angry shock,
in vain the drifting sands:
unharmed upon the eternal Rock
the eternal city stands.

하나님의 도시여, 그대의 성벽은 얼마나 넓고 아득한가
장엄하게 펼쳐진 그대의 벽들아!
모든 시대와 땅의 참된 그대 자유인의 권리가 있으니:

하나의 거룩한 교회, 하나의 강한 군대,
변함없고 고귀한 한 뜻;
한 갈래의 일꾼 무리, 한 곡의 거둠의 노래,
전능하신 한 왕.

그대의 말은 얼마나 순수하게 인류의 태초의 젊음으로부터 전해졌는가!
그대의 제국은 얼마나 장엄하게 자라났는가
자유와 사랑과 진리의 세계로!

밤새 절대 꺼지지 않는 광채로 그대의 봉화는 어떻게도 빛나는가!
고요하고 빛나는 그대의 탑들은 어떻게도 솟아오르는가,
새벽을 맞이하러!

파도의 성난 충격도 헛되니,
떠내려가는 모래도 헛되도다:
영원한 반석 위에 해를 입지 않고
영원한 도시는 서 있도다.

What do we think about when we think of the term ‘church’? We live in a day when there are many and varied churches. If one church doesn’t suit you, there are others to choose from. While some churches encourage their people to live for God and others instead of themselves, other churches promote a gospel that says lots of money and a better life now are the results of following Christ. However, there are still churches that try to follow what the Bible says—Sola scriptura (scripture alone). Traditionally, the conservative Anabaptist churches in America have tried to function in this manner. But is that changing?

We live in a day when lines are being crossed, blurred, and confused. People aren’t sure what is true and what is not. Today, men and women around the world are looking for answers and solutions, but where should they look?

I was talking with a young man who testified of being converted at a young age. He attended church faithfully and was considered quite gifted. But there was a problem—he had a sin that he still could not control. As he wrestled with God and pled for victory, he began to hear a recurring message from other professing Christians, “No one is perfect!” “We all have issues.” “Everyone has sinned!” Finally, this young man accepted his sin as normal. He justified it because it seemed that everyone was saying they had sin also, that they were not living in complete victory. It led this young man to a place of complete ruin.

Are we preaching and accepting a defeated Gospel—a gospel that doesn’t offer complete forgiveness and complete victory? Many youth of today are confused. Many people in today’s world don’t understand. Anyone can go to church and try to be a better person. But what about the all-powerful, life-changing gospel of Jesus Christ?

The apostle Paul says that Jesus is coming back for “. . .a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5:27). And Jesus Himself said “. . .That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18).

Before I was converted, I was certainly a slave to sin, but I wanted victory. I was addicted to drugs and alcohol, but I didn’t like it. I wanted to be free. I went to counseling and rehab facilities all over America, but it didn’t work. I had no power. I could quit for a few days or even weeks, then anger and depression would set in, and I would return to the substances. One day, I came face to face with the Creator. The hand of the almighty God got ahold of me and opened my eyes. I repented of my sins and was given a clean slate and a clean heart. I never went back. Drugs, alcohol, and two packs of cigarettes a day were finished—forever.

I could hardly believe what God was doing. The power of God was real. I could not overcome it by myself, as none of us can, but God has promised us freedom from bondage and a new life of victorious living if we submit our lives to him. This ability to overcome the power of sin and then walk in victory is what the world is looking for. Do we believe that God can free us not only from substance abuse but also from anger, selfishness, bitterness, greed, and pride? God’s Word says “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). No one is interested in a defeated Gospel, no one except those who are living in defeat because they have chosen the things of this world over God and His Word.

Are we willing to testify of the power of the resurrection? We need to proclaim a gospel that completely saves people from the bondage of sin—forever. We must be bold and confident in our faith so we can lead people to the Master.

I was witnessing to a man when he said in a rather loud voice, “God is not real!” My six-year-old son’s mouth fell open, and he gasped, “Daddy, he just told a lie!”

My son doesn’t need to be convinced that God is real; he believes it with all his heart. The world out there does need to be convinced. They need to see something that science cannot explain. They need to see something that defies all odds.

That something is a heart that has been truly changed. The fighter now loves his enemies. The person with an anger problem now loves others unconditionally. Broken families are healed. Wretched sinners are forgiven and living a transformed life. Hope, peace, love, and power are freely given to men and women who seemingly have no hope. “The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them ” (Matt. 11:5).

Are you living your life so the world can see the work of God being practical, effective, and real every day? Here are a few things the Church needs in our day to once again draw in the lost.

A willingness to suffer

History would show that the church, all through the ages, has suffered for Christ. It was part of the cost of following Christ. The Bible says, “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). It was something that just happened.

Today, many people want the American dream. Folks live a good moral life, are good citizens, make a good living, and go to church on Sundays. But is that what we are called to? The gospel spread like wildfire when the church suffered persecution and did so willingly and joyfully. It was something the world had never seen—a faith that people showed by their life, and their death was something worth dying for. Let’s not be afraid to suffer for Christ today.

Denial of self

Then said Jesus unto his disciples, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

Have you ever wondered why Jesus instructs us to deny ourselves? After all, He gave us desires and passions, so why must we deny them? I have heard people say that we need to align our will with God’s, but I do not find this in the Bible. Rather, we should simply deny our will and accept God’s will.

I remember the first day of boot camp when I joined the Marine Corps after graduating from high school. Close to one hundred young men were there. We all had our own desires and thoughts. We had our own identity. It was amazing to see all the diversity. It would have been a disaster if the United States of America had sent us off to battle that first day. So, they had a plan set in place to fix this problem. Over the next three months, they broke us. Physically and mentally, we learned how to deny ourselves and submit to our commanders and each other. The world is often amazed by the great discipline and unity for which the Marines are known.

When we become a part of the kingdom of God, we cannot be effective if we each do what we want. A body of believers can all have good intentions, but if any one person has not denied themselves, they will never be able to submit to the greater cause. There is a war raging, and we cannot fight it alone. We must deny ourselves, join forces with our brethren, and fight for victory in our homes, churches, and lives.

Submission

The Bible calls us to submit ourselves:

  • to God (Jas. 4:7).
  • [to those] that have the [spiritual] rule over you [us] (Heb. 13:17).
  • to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake (1 Pet. 2:13).
  • one to another in the fear of God (Eph. 5:21).

Once we deny ourselves, then and only then, can we submit to others. Many people today have great difficulty in submitting to their fellow man. Some feel they are free in Christ; therefore, they can do as they please. There is a reason why we are instructed to submit to others. It is easy for us to drift away from sound doctrine when we believe we can figure everything out on our own.

When we have truly denied ourselves, we find that it is rather easy, and even a great blessing, to submit to the brotherhood. In fact, it is true freedom. What you want doesn’t matter, and you begin to depend on your brothers and sisters. When getting our own way isn’t important to us, then when we don’t get our way, we are fine with it. As we lay down our lives for each other, we become a force that the world doesn’t understand. The world was drawn to the church for centuries, wanting what it had. But amazingly, today, it seems the church is being drawn to the world, wanting what it has.

There is power in submission. Hundreds of years ago, a man named Alexander the Great conquered almost all of the then-known world using military strength and cleverness mixed with diplomacy.

The story is told that Alexander and a small company of soldiers approached a strongly fortified, walled city. Standing outside the walls, Alexander raised his voice and demanded to see the king. When the king arrived, Alexander insisted that the king surrender the city and its inhabitants to Alexander and his little band of fighting men.

The king laughed, “Why should I surrender to you? You can’t do us any harm!” So, Alexander offered to give the king a demonstration. He ordered his men to line up single file and start marching. He marched them straight toward a sheer cliff.

The townspeople gathered on the wall and watched in shocked silence as, one by one, Alexander’s soldiers marched, without hesitation, right off the cliff to their deaths! After ten soldiers died, Alexander ordered the rest of the men to return to his side. The townspeople and the king immediately surrendered to Alexander the Great. They realized that if a few men were actually willing to commit suicide at the command of this dynamic leader, then nothing could stop his eventual victory.

Obedience

Submission and obedience go hand in hand. If we are willing to submit to something or someone, we will want to obey it. It becomes very important to submit to those who are over us, especially the almighty God in Heaven. If we struggle to submit, we will usually struggle with obedience. God forbid if we begin to believe that we are better off doing things alone without our brothers.

Love

“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (John 13:35).

People wave to each other at an intersection, or they will open the door for an elderly person. People are generally loving people until something doesn’t go their way. Then they can become very difficult. Is that the way the church today is showing its love to the world? As long as everything is going smoothly, and no one steps on our toes, we all get along and we love each other. Then as soon as there is something worth fighting over, we put the “boxing gloves” on. Doesn’t the Bible say that “charity (love) beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things” (1 Cor. 13:7)? True love is revealed when we face adversity or when a brother does something to offend us. That is the love that will show the world we are disciples of Jesus.

Do we love our brother enough to help when he is in need? Maybe he is unknowingly straying away from God in a certain area. How much do we love him? Some people think that love is only talking about positive things with each other, but if we truly love our brother, we will go to him in love and speak honestly with him. Then if we are practicing a lifestyle of denying ourselves and submitting to the brethren, it should go well. God forbid if we get angry with a brother who comes to us to show us our error.

When we have chosen to suffer with the people of God and have denied ourselves, then we appreciate when a brother or sister speaks into our lives. We will not allow ourselves to become offended.

Suffering for and with each other, plus denying ourselves for each other, often forms a solid love for one another. This type of love is the kind that the world around us does not know but desires greatly. The world is getting more selfish and independent as the days pass. We can’t afford to miss our opportunities to show them the power of God with our love for one another.

Godly people throughout the ages have had their opportunity to serve the King and spread the message of the Kingdom of God, but they have moved on to eternity. Today it is our turn. The fields are white unto harvest. Let’s plug in and, with God’s help, preserve the glorious church of Jesus Christ for our children, the next generation.

À quoi pensons-nous quand nous entendons le terme « église » ? Nous vivons à une époque où il existe de nombreuses églises, variées. Si une église ne vous convient pas, il y en a d’autres à choisir. Tandis que certaines églises encouragent leurs membres à vivre pour Dieu et pour les autres plutôt que pour eux-mêmes, d’autres promeuvent un évangile qui affirme qu’une grande richesse et une vie meilleure dès maintenant sont les résultats du fait de suivre Christ. Toutefois, il existe encore des églises qui tentent de suivre ce que dit la Bible—Sola scriptura (les Écritures seules). Traditionnellement, les églises anabaptistes conservatrices en Amérique ont essayé de fonctionner de cette manière. Mais cela est-il en train de changer ?

Nous vivons à une époque où les lignes sont franchies, brouillées et confondues. Les gens ne savent pas ce qui est vrai et ce qui ne l’est pas. Aujourd’hui, des hommes et des femmes partout dans le monde cherchent des réponses et des solutions, mais où doivent-ils les chercher ?

Je parlais avec un jeune homme qui témoignait avoir été converti dès son jeune âge. Il fréquentait l’église assidûment et on le jugeait assez doué. Mais il y avait un problème—il avait un péché qu’il ne pouvait toujours pas maîtriser. Alors qu’il luttait avec Dieu et suppliait pour la victoire, il a commencé à entendre un message récurrent d’autres chrétiens qui se professent tels, « Personne n’est parfait ! » « Nous avons tous des problèmes. » « Tout le monde a péché ! » Finalement, ce jeune homme a accepté son péché comme normal. Il l’a justifié parce qu’il semblait que tout le monde disait qu’il avait aussi du péché, qu’ils ne vivaient pas dans la victoire complète. Cela a conduit ce jeune homme à un lieu de ruine complète.

Prêchons-nous et acceptons-nous un Évangile vaincu—un évangile qui n’offre pas le pardon complet et la victoire complète ? Beaucoup de jeunes aujourd’hui sont confus. Beaucoup de gens dans le monde d’aujourd’hui ne comprennent pas. N’importe qui peut aller à l’église et essayer d’être une meilleure personne. Mais qu’en est-il de l’évangile tout-puissant et qui change la vie de Jésus-Christ ?

L’apôtre Paul dit que Jésus revient pour « …une église glorieuse, sans tache, ni ride, ni rien de semblable; mais qu’elle soit sainte et irrépréhensible » (Eph. 5:27). Et Jésus Lui-même a dit « …Tu es Pierre, et sur cette pierre je bâtirai mon Église; et les portes du séjour des morts ne prévaudront point contre elle » (Matt. 16:18).

Avant ma conversion, j’étais certes esclave du péché, mais je voulais la victoire. J’étais accro aux drogues et à l’alcool, mais je n’aimais pas cela. Je voulais être libre. Je suis allé en conseil et dans des centres de rééducation partout en Amérique, mais cela n’a pas marché. Je n’avais aucun pouvoir. Je pouvais arrêter pendant quelques jours ou même des semaines, puis la colère et la dépression revenaient, et je retournais aux substances. Un jour, je me suis retrouvé face à face avec le Créateur. La main du Dieu tout-puissant m’a saisi et m’a ouvert les yeux. Je me suis repenti de mes péchés et on m’a donné une ardoise propre et un cœur pur. Je ne suis jamais retourné en arrière. Les drogues, l’alcool et deux paquets de cigarettes par jour étaient terminés—pour toujours.

J’avais du mal à croire ce que Dieu faisait. La puissance de Dieu était réelle. Je ne pouvais pas la vaincre par moi-même, comme aucun de nous ne le peut, mais Dieu nous a promis la liberté de l’esclavage et une nouvelle vie de marche victorieuse si nous soumettons nos vies à lui. Cette capacité de vaincre la puissance du péché puis de marcher dans la victoire est ce que le monde recherche. Croyons-nous que Dieu peut nous libérer non seulement de l’abus de substances mais aussi de la colère, de l’égoïsme, de l’amertume, de la cupidité et de l’orgueil ? La Parole de Dieu dit « Si nous confessons nos péchés, il est fidèle et juste pour nous les pardonner, et pour nous purifier de toute iniquité » (1 John 1:9). Personne n’est intéressé par un Évangile vaincu, personne sauf ceux qui vivent dans la défaite parce qu’ils ont choisi les choses de ce monde au lieu de Dieu et de Sa Parole.

Sommes-nous prêts à témoigner de la puissance de la résurrection ? Nous devons proclamer un évangile qui sauve complètement les gens de l’esclavage du péché—pour toujours. Nous devons être hardis et confiants dans notre foi afin de conduire les gens vers le Maître.

Je témoignais à un homme quand il a dit d’une voix plutôt forte : « Dieu n’est pas réel ! » La bouche de mon fils de six ans s’est ouverte, et il a poussé un cri : « Papa, il vient de dire un mensonge ! »

Mon fils n’a pas besoin d’être convaincu que Dieu est réel ; il le croit de tout son cœur. Le monde dehors a besoin d’être convaincu. Il doit voir quelque chose que la science ne peut pas expliquer. Il doit voir quelque chose qui défie toute probabilité.

Ce quelque chose est un cœur qui a été véritablement changé. Le combattant aime maintenant ses ennemis. La personne qui avait un problème de colère aime maintenant les autres inconditionnellement. Les familles brisées sont guéries. Des pécheurs misérables sont pardonnés et vivent une vie transformée. L’espérance, la paix, l’amour et la puissance sont offertes gratuitement à des hommes et des femmes qui apparemment n’ont aucun espoir. « Les aveugles recouvrent la vue, et les boiteux marchent, les lépreux sont purifiés, et les sourds entendent, les morts ressuscitent, et la bonne nouvelle est annoncée aux pauvres » (Matt. 11:5).

Vivez-vous votre vie de sorte que le monde puisse voir l’œuvre de Dieu comme pratique, efficace et réelle chaque jour ? Voici quelques choses dont l’Église a besoin à notre époque pour attirer à nouveau les perdus.

Une volonté de souffrir

L’histoire montre que l’église, à travers les âges, a souffert pour Christ. Cela faisait partie du coût de suivre Christ. La Bible dit : « Et tous ceux qui veulent vivre pieusement en Jésus-Christ seront persécutés » (2 Tim. 3:12). C’était quelque chose qui arrivait tout simplement.

Aujourd’hui, beaucoup de gens veulent le rêve américain. Les gens mènent une bonne vie morale, sont de bons citoyens, gagnent bien leur vie et vont à l’église le dimanche. Mais est-ce ce à quoi nous sommes appelés ? L’évangile s’est répandu comme une traînée de poudre lorsque l’église a souffert la persécution et l’a fait volontairement et joyeusement. C’était quelque chose que le monde n’avait jamais vu—une foi que les gens montraient par leur vie, et leur mort était quelque chose pour lequel il valait la peine de mourir. N’ayons pas peur de souffrir pour Christ aujourd’hui.

Renoncement à soi

Puis Jésus dit à ses disciples : « Si quelqu’un veut venir après moi, qu’il renonce à lui-même, qu’il se charge de sa croix, et qu’il me suive » (Matt. 16:24).

Vous êtes-vous déjà demandé pourquoi Jésus nous enjoint de renoncer à nous-mêmes ? Après tout, Il nous a donnés des désirs et des passions, alors pourquoi devons‑nous les renier ? J’ai entendu des gens dire que nous devons aligner notre volonté sur celle de Dieu, mais je ne trouve pas cela dans la Bible. Au contraire, nous devons simplement renoncer à notre volonté et accepter la volonté de Dieu.

Je me souviens du premier jour du camp d’entraînement quand j’ai rejoint le Corps des Marines après avoir obtenu mon diplôme d’études secondaires. Près d’une centaine de jeunes hommes étaient là. Nous avions tous nos propres désirs et pensées. Nous avions notre propre identité. C’était étonnant de voir toute cette diversité. Cela aurait été un désastre si les États-Unis d’Amérique nous avaient envoyés au combat ce premier jour. Alors, ils avaient un plan en place pour résoudre ce problème. Au cours des trois mois suivants, ils nous ont brisés. Physiquement et mentalement, nous avons appris à nous renier et à nous soumettre à nos commandants et les uns aux autres. Le monde est souvent étonné par la grande discipline et l’unité qui font la réputation des Marines.

Quand nous devenons partie du royaume de Dieu, nous ne pouvons pas être efficaces si chacun fait ce qu’il veut. Un corps de croyants peut tous avoir de bonnes intentions, mais si une seule personne n’a pas renoncé à elle-même, elle ne pourra jamais se soumettre à la cause plus grande. Il y a une guerre en cours, et nous ne pouvons pas la mener seuls. Nous devons nous renier, nous unir à nos frères, et nous battre pour la victoire dans nos foyers, nos églises et nos vies.

Soumission

La Bible nous appelle à nous soumettre :

  • à Dieu (Jas. 4:7).
  • [à ceux] qui ont la domination [spirituelle] sur vous [nous] (Heb. 13:17).
  • à toute institution humaine, pour l’amour du Seigneur (1 Pet. 2:13).
  • les uns aux autres dans la crainte de Dieu (Eph. 5:21).

Une fois que nous nous renions, alors et seulement alors, pouvons-nous nous soumettre aux autres. Beaucoup de gens aujourd’hui ont de grandes difficultés à se soumettre à leur semblable. Certains pensent qu’ils sont libres en Christ ; par conséquent, ils peuvent faire ce qu’ils veulent. Il y a une raison pour laquelle nous sommes instruits à nous soumettre aux autres. Il est facile pour nous de dériver de la saine doctrine quand nous croyons que nous pouvons tout comprendre par nous-mêmes.

Quand nous nous sommes réellement reniés, nous trouvons qu’il est assez facile, et même une grande bénédiction, de nous soumettre à la fraternité. En fait, c’est la vraie liberté. Ce que vous voulez n’a pas d’importance, et vous commencez à dépendre de vos frères et sœurs. Quand obtenir son propre chemin n’est plus important pour nous, alors, lorsque nous ne l’obtenons pas, cela nous convient. Tandis que nous posons nos vies les uns pour les autres, nous devenons une force que le monde ne comprend pas. Le monde a été attiré vers l’église pendant des siècles, désirant ce qu’elle avait. Mais étonnamment, aujourd’hui, il semble que l’église soit attirée vers le monde, désirant ce qu’il a.

Il y a du pouvoir dans la soumission. Il y a des centaines d’années, un homme nommé Alexandre le Grand conquit presque tout le monde alors connu en utilisant la force militaire et l’intelligence mêlées à la diplomatie.

On raconte qu’Alexandre et une petite compagnie de soldats approchèrent une ville fortement fortifiée, entourée de murs. Debout à l’extérieur des murs, Alexandre éleva la voix et exigea de voir le roi. Lorsque le roi arriva, Alexandre insista pour que le roi rende la ville et ses habitants à Alexandre et à sa petite troupe de soldats.

Le roi rit : « Pourquoi devrais‑je me rendre à toi ? Tu ne peux rien nous faire ! » Alors Alexandre proposa de donner une démonstration. Il ordonna à ses hommes de se mettre en file indienne et de commencer à marcher. Il les fit marcher droit vers une falaise abrupte.

Les habitants se rassemblèrent sur le mur et regardèrent en silence, choqués, tandis que, un par un, les soldats d’Alexandre marchaient, sans hésiter, tout droit hors de la falaise jusqu’à leur mort ! Après dix soldats morts, Alexandre ordonna au reste des hommes de revenir à ses côtés. Les habitants et le roi se rendirent immédiatement à Alexandre le Grand. Ils réalisèrent que si quelques hommes étaient réellement prêts à commettre un suicide sur commandement de ce chef dynamique, alors rien ne pourrait arrêter sa victoire éventuelle.

Obéissance

Soumission et obéissance vont de pair. Si nous sommes prêts à nous soumettre à quelque chose ou à quelqu’un, nous voudrons lui obéir. Il devient très important de se soumettre à ceux qui sont au‑dessus de nous, particulièrement au Dieu tout‑puissant au Ciel. Si nous peinons à nous soumettre, nous aurons généralement du mal avec l’obéissance. Dieu nous en préserve si nous commençons à croire que nous sommes mieux à faire les choses seuls sans nos frères.

Amour

« A ceci tous connaîtront que vous êtes mes disciples, si vous avez de l’amour les uns pour les autres » (John 13:35).

Les gens se saluent au coin de la rue, ou ils ouvriront la porte à une personne âgée. Les gens sont généralement aimants jusqu’à ce que quelque chose ne tourne pas en leur faveur. Alors ils peuvent devenir très difficiles. Est‑ce ainsi que l’église montre aujourd’hui son amour au monde ? Tant que tout va bien et que personne ne nous marche sur les pieds, nous nous entendons tous et nous nous aimons. Puis dès qu’il y a quelque chose pour lequel il vaut la peine de se battre, nous enfilons les « gants de boxe ». La Bible ne dit‑elle pas que « la charité (l’amour) couvre tout, croit tout, espère tout, endure tout » (1 Cor. 13:7) ? Le véritable amour se révèle quand nous faisons face à l’adversité ou lorsqu’un frère nous offense. C’est cet amour qui montrera au monde que nous sommes des disciples de Jésus.

Aimons‑nous notre frère suffisamment pour l’aider quand il est dans le besoin ? Peut‑être s’éloigne‑t‑il sans le savoir de Dieu dans un certain domaine. Combien l’aimons‑nous ? Certaines personnes pensent que l’amour consiste seulement à parler des choses positives entre nous, mais si nous aimons vraiment notre frère, nous irons vers lui avec amour et lui parlerons franchement. Ensuite, si nous pratiquons un style de vie de renoncement à soi et de soumission à la fraternité, cela devrait bien se passer. Dieu nous en préserve si nous nous mettons en colère contre un frère qui vient pour nous montrer notre erreur.

Quand nous avons choisi de souffrir avec le peuple de Dieu et nous être reniés, alors nous apprécions lorsqu’un frère ou une sœur vient parler dans nos vies. Nous ne nous permettrons pas d’être offensés.

Souffrir pour et avec les autres, plus se renier pour les autres, forme souvent un amour solide les uns pour les autres. Ce type d’amour est celui que le monde qui nous entoure ne connaît pas mais désire ardemment. Le monde devient de plus en plus égoïste et indépendant au fil des jours. Nous ne pouvons pas nous permettre de manquer nos occasions de leur montrer la puissance de Dieu par notre amour les uns pour les autres.

Les personnes pieuses à travers les âges ont eu leur opportunité de servir le Roi et de répandre le message du Royaume de Dieu, mais elles sont passées à l’éternité. Aujourd’hui, c’est notre tour. Les champs sont blancs pour la moisson. Branchons‑nous et, avec l’aide de Dieu, préservons l’église glorieuse de Jésus‑Christ pour nos enfants, la prochaine génération.
